title: Find which prospects run Shopify, HubSpot or Microsoft 365, from a list of domains
summary:
A lot of B2B selling starts with "what do they run?". A Shopify app developer wants the stores on Shopify, an agency wants the sites with no ad pixel, an email security vendor wants the companies on Microsoft 365 without a DMARC policy. The answer is sitting in each company's homepage and DNS records; reading it for a few thousand domains by hand is the problem.

This post turns a domain list into a segmented prospect sheet in Python, then compares the tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Tech Stack API. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

What one row tells you

Each domain is read live: its homepage once (robots.txt obeyed) and its public MX, SPF, DMARC and NS records. One row per domain:

  • One column per category, as a list of names: cms, ecommerce, analytics, tag_manager, advertising (Meta Pixel, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok...), chat, crm_marketing, payments, consent, framework, backend, web_server, cdn_hosting.
  • Email from DNS: email_provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Zoho...), email_security (a gateway such as Mimecast or Proofpoint), email_sender (sending services named in SPF), dmarc_policy (none, quarantine or reject), plus the raw mx and spf.

title: Parsing SEC EDGAR Facts: Reconciling Cash Flow with Python
summary:
Financial data engineering pipelines often focus heavily on headline metrics such as Revenue and Net Income. However, when evaluating the structural cash generation of corporate disclosures, relying solely on top-line and bottom-line GAAP figures presents an incomplete picture. In corporate filings submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Statement of Cash Flows provides the vital reconciliation connecting book accruals to actual cash inflows and outflows.

For developers and data engineers building disclosure parsers, extracting and reconciling these line items programmatically can be tricky. Company reporting structures utilize the US-GAAP XBRL taxonomy, where line items represent time intervals, instant snapshots, or custom extensions. In this guide, we walk through building a Python script to fetch, parse, and reconcile Operating Cash Flow adjustments directly from the public SEC EDGAR API.

The Architecture of SEC EDGAR Facts API

The SEC provides a programmatic API that exposes structured XBRL data directly in JSON format via its EDGAR system. Instead of scraping multi-megabyte HTML tables and wrestling with irregular regex patterns, developers can query the companyfacts endpoint:

https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK{cik_10_digits}.json

To interact with this API, the SEC enforces two primary architectural rules:

  1. User-Agent Compliance: Requests must provide a descriptive User-Agent header containing the user's name and contact email (for example, DataPipeline/1.0 developer@example.com). Anonymous or generic user agents receive immediate HTTP 403 Forbidden errors.
  2. Fair Access Rate Limiting: Applications must not exceed 10 requests per second.

The returned JSON payload organizes reported financial concepts under standard taxonomies—primarily us-gaap and dei (Document and Entity Information). Within each concept, disclosures are structured by currency unit (e.g., USD) containing an array of filing objects.

Why Reconciliations Matter: A Real-World Example

Consider a high-growth tech enterprise filing Form 10-Q. In Qualcomm Incorporated's Form 10-Q for the six months ended March 29, 2026 (CIK 0000804328, Accession Number 0000804328-26-000061), headline GAAP Net Income was reported at $10.375 billion, while Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities was $7.414 billion.

This represents a divergence of -$2.961 billion. Headline earnings were substantially higher than cash collected from operations. Why?

  • Share-Based Compensation: A non-cash expense of $1.749 billion added back to cash flow.
  • Depreciation & Amortization: A non-cash expense of $806 million added back.
  • Cash Tax Adjustments and Working Capital: Substantial timing differences between accrued income tax provisions and actual cash tax disbursements, alongside operational receivable shifts.

Automating the extraction of these reconciling line items allows quantitative pipelines to monitor earning quality automatically.

Implementing the Python Extractor

Below is a complete, self-contained Python implementation utilizing Python's standard library modules (urllib, gzip, and json). It fetches raw company facts, extracts targeted US-GAAP concepts, filters by SEC accession number, and computes the net operating cash flow divergence.

import gzip
import json
import urllib.request
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional


def fetch_company_facts(cik: str, user_agent: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Fetch structured XBRL company facts from the SEC EDGAR API."""
    cik_padded = cik.strip().zfill(10)
    url = f"https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK{cik_padded}.json"
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        headers={"User-Agent": user_agent, "Accept-Encoding": "gzip, deflate"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as response:
        raw_bytes = response.read()
        if (
            response.info().get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip"
            or raw_bytes[:2] == b"\x1f\x8b"
        ):
            raw_bytes = gzip.decompress(raw_bytes)
        return json.loads(raw_bytes.decode("utf-8"))


def get_fact_value(
    facts_data: Dict[str, Any],
    taxonomy: str,
    concept: str,
    accession_number: str,
    start_date: str,
    end_date: str,
) -> Optional[float]:
    """Extract a specific concept value by accession number and period."""
    concept_entry = (
        facts_data.get("facts", {}).get(taxonomy, {}).get(concept, {})
    )
    units = concept_entry.get("units", {})

    for unit_key, records in units.items():
        for record in records:
            if (
                record.get("accn") == accession_number
                and record.get("start") == start_date
                and record.get("end") == end_date
            ):
                return float(record.get("val", 0.0))
    return None


def main() -> None:
    # SEC EDGAR CIK for Qualcomm Incorporated
    cik = "0000804328"
    user_agent = "DataEngineeringTutorial/1.0 (dev@example.com)"

    # Form 10-Q period parameters: 6M FY2026 (ended March 29, 2026)
    accession = "0000804328-26-000061"
    start_date = "2025-09-29"
    end_date = "2026-03-29"

    print(f"Querying SEC EDGAR facts for CIK {cik}...")
    facts = fetch_company_facts(cik, user_agent)
    company_name = facts.get("entityName", "Unknown Entity")
    print(f"Retrieved disclosures for: {company_name}")

    # Extract core cash flow reconciliation concepts
    net_income = get_fact_value(
        facts, "us-gaap", "NetIncomeLoss", accession, start_date, end_date
    )
    operating_cf = get_fact_value(
        facts,
        "us-gaap",
        "NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivities",
        accession,
        start_date,
        end_date,
    )
    sbc = get_fact_value(
        facts,
        "us-gaap",
        "ShareBasedCompensation",
        accession,
        start_date,
        end_date,
    )
    depr_amort = get_fact_value(
        facts,
        "us-gaap",
        "DepreciationDepletionAndAmortization",
        accession,
        start_date,
        end_date,
    )

    print("\n--- Statement of Cash Flows Extraction ---")
    print(f"Net Income:                       ${net_income:,.0f}")
    print(f"Operating Cash Flow:              ${operating_cf:,.0f}")
    print(f"Share-Based Compensation Addback: ${sbc:,.0f}")
    print(f"Depreciation & Amortization:      ${depr_amort:,.0f}")

    if net_income is not None and operating_cf is not None:
        divergence = operating_cf - net_income
        print(f"\nNet Divergence (OCF - Net Income): ${divergence:,.0f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Critical Financial Data Engineering Pitfalls

When operationalizing XBRL extraction scripts into production pipelines, keep these three edge cases in mind:

  1. Duration vs. Instant Concepts: Balance sheet metrics (such as Assets or CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue) represent a specific point in time and only contain an end date key. Income statement and cash flow items represent a duration, requiring matching on both start and end dates. If your parser ignores the start date, it may inadvertently pull a 3-month quarterly figure instead of a 6-month or 9-month year-to-date figure.

  2. Accession Number Matching (accn): Companies frequently revise or reclassify prior-year comparisons in subsequent filings. Filtering strictly by fiscal year (fy) or period (fp) can yield multiple conflicting values across different filing dates. Keying records directly to the accession number (accn) guarantees that all retrieved line items come from the identical filing submission.

  3. Accrual vs. Cash Accounting Line Meanings: Accounting reconciliation labels require precise parsing. For example, a cash flow adjustment line labelled “income tax provision less than income tax payments” is an accrual adjustment reflecting the delta between recognized tax expense and actual cash paid. It is not the total cash tax payment itself. Automated systems should label adjustments accurately to avoid distorting downstream financial models.

Conclusion

Automating financial disclosure processing with the SEC EDGAR API removes the fragility of web scraping. By leveraging standard US-GAAP concepts, strictly isolating accession numbers, and respecting duration scopes, data engineers can reliably compute cash flow reconciliations and track corporate cash dynamics at scale.

Automating financial disclosure processing with the SEC EDGAR API removes the fragility of web scraping. title: Treat a crawler skill's output as a versioned interface
summary:
A saved crawler workflow is easier to reuse when the next person can trust its output shape. Finding the same button again is only part of the job. Downstream code still needs stable field names, clear missing values, and a way to distinguish a complete collection from an interrupted one.

Here is a small contract I would put around a reusable extraction skill. It is an application-side design example, not a BrowserAct API, a generated Skill Forge artifact, or a claim that a real website passed these checks. This article comes from the BrowserAct team.

Write the consumer's assumptions first

Start with the code or person receiving the result. Which fields identify a row? Which values may be absent? What does the caller do when pagination stops early?

For a directory collection, a consumer might require a source-specific record ID and a source URL. A contact email could remain null when it was not visible. The workflow should not invent a value simply because an export column exists.

Decide those rules before saving the skill. Otherwise a changed extraction path can return plausible JSON that quietly breaks an importer.

Separate shape from coverage

Consider this fictional response:

{
  "schema_version": "records.v1",
  "stop_reason": "row_limit",
  "rows": [
    {
      "record_id": "demo-17",
      "source_url": "https://example.com/records/demo-17",
      "email": null
    }
  ]
}

The response can be structurally valid while covering only part of the requested data. A row limit is an intentional stop, not proof that the directory ended. A blocked page is another reason to return a partial collection with an explicit status.

Use a separate coverage check when you have an authoritative expected set. Without that set, report what was observed and how traversal ended. Do not infer completeness from the absence of an exception.

Put a small validator at the boundary

The following Python example checks a deliberately narrow contract. It does not fetch a website, validate that a URL belongs to the requested source, or prove that row values are true.

def validate_result(result):
    if not isinstance(result, dict):
        raise ValueError("result must be an object")
    if result.get("schema_version") != "records.v1":
        raise ValueError("unsupported schema version")
    if result.get("stop_reason") not in {
        "exhausted", "row_limit", "blocked"
    }:
        raise ValueError("unknown stop reason")
    rows = result.get("rows")
    if not isinstance(rows, list):
        raise ValueError("rows must be a list")
    seen = set()
    for index, row in enumerate(rows):
        if not isinstance(row, dict):
            raise ValueError(f"row {index} must be an object")
        for field in ("record_id", "source_url"):
            value = row.get(field)
            if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
                raise ValueError(f"row {index}: missing {field}")
        key = row["record_id"].strip()
        if key in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate record_id: {key}")
        seen.add(key)
    return result

Here, IDs are unique within this one result. A cross-source collection would need a key that includes the source identity. Do not copy this deduplication rule into a different dataset without checking what makes a record unique.

The validator permits additional fields so optional additions do not automatically break this consumer. It also permits an empty list. Whether an empty collection is an acceptable business result belongs in the coverage and acceptance rules, not in a guessed minimum row count.

Test the contract without pretending to test the crawler

Before connecting it to an importer, try synthetic fixtures: a valid response, a partial blocked response, an empty response, a duplicate ID, a missing source URL, an unsupported version, and a non-list rows value.

The last four should be rejected by this validator. The first three should pass shape validation, with their different business meanings preserved. Passing these fixtures establishes the behavior of this local check. It says nothing about browser access, pagination correctness, or extraction accuracy on a live portal.

Then test the actual saved skill separately, with authorized access and new inputs. Inspect source evidence as well as the returned structure. Keep those results distinct from the synthetic checks.

Version meaning changes, not only field names

A change from a local record ID to a global identifier may keep the same JSON type while changing the meaning. Changing a date from local time to UTC can do the same thing. Treat those changes as contract decisions.

Record the skill revision and contract version with each run. When introducing a breaking change, retain a representative old result and exercise the migration before replacing the importer. A version label is useful only when consumers actually check it.

For missing optional values, document whether null means not observed, unavailable, or not applicable. If your business needs those distinctions, add a separate status field rather than overloading null with several incompatible meanings.

Our Skill Forge workflow guide discusses turning exploration into something reusable. An output contract gives the next caller a concrete boundary to review, even when the website path changes.

Which breaks your downstream pipeline more often: changed fields, duplicate records, or an incomplete collection that looked successful?

title: Ming-3.0-tts on a 16 GB card: the GPU sat mostly idle, and why a bigger one barely helps
summary:
When a speech model runs slower than real time, the reflex is to rent a bigger GPU. With Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B that buys very little. An RTX 2000 Ada sat idle more than two thirds of the time. An RTX 4090 worked at most one moment in five, and the speedup was about 17%.

The model comes from the inclusionAI team at Ant Group. They released weights and code under MIT, with their own benchmarks and a frank list of limitations. It copies a voice from a few seconds of sample audio, builds one from a text prompt describing it, and turns inline tags like [Laughter] or [Sigh] into sounds. Their model page only mentions H800-80GB and H20-96G cards, with no memory figure. We ran their unmodified code on a small card to get one. Every number is in our Ming-3.0-tts memory and speed test on an RTX 2000 Ada.

Low GPU utilisation is the first thing to check

"Real time" is a ratio: seconds of audio produced per second of compute. A 20.7-second English paragraph cost 31 to 32 seconds on the RTX 2000 Ada. On the 4090, a 20.9-second paragraph cost 27 seconds. Its faster host processor may explain part of that gain.

The culprit is the decode loop, which builds the audio step by step, 80 milliseconds per step. Between steps, Python code on the CPU prepares and launches the next one. Keeping up with playback takes 12.5 steps per second. We measured about 8.3 to 8.9. The GPU is a fast bus stuck behind a slow ticket check at every stop.

Before sizing hardware for a text-to-speech (TTS) model, run nvidia-smi while it speaks and read utilisation, the share of time the GPU is working. If it stays low, a faster card will not buy you speed. One possible way out, untested by us: vLLM-Omni, an engine built for fast serving, which Ming's roadmap marks as supported.

Emulate the small card before you rent it

No real card below 16 GB ran. Two 12 GB RTX 3080 Ti machines booted without the SSH access our installer needs, and no 8 GB card was available to rent. So we faked one. PyTorch, the library Ming runs on, has a call, torch.cuda.set_per_process_memory_fraction, that limits how much GPU memory the process may take. We lowered it on the 16 GB card until loading broke.

With caps of 8, 4 and 3 GiB, the output WAVs had the same md5 checksum as the uncapped run, and speed did not change. At 2.75 GiB, setup died with "CUDA out of memory". Add roughly 0.4 GB for the driver and the article's estimate lands at a 4 GB card. Nobody ran that on real hardware, and a smaller chip may also be slower.

Copy the hashing habit: loading under a cap proves little, matching bytes prove the cap changed nothing.

Log the timings with every request

Our custom backend, a short Python file that wraps the authors' code behind an HTTP API, returns its own measurements next to the audio. This came back for a cloned line with three tags on the RTX 2000 Ada:

"timings": { "gpu_s": 11.02, "realtime_factor": 0.63, "peak_vram_mib": 2922 }

That request spent 11.02 seconds of GPU time on 7.0 seconds of audio. Strip the tags and the same line took 8.05 seconds for 5.3 seconds of audio. Tags are extra sound, and sound costs time. Log these fields from day one.

Three traps you will hit

  • Numbers. Before speaking, English text goes through normalisation, a step that spells numbers and symbols out as words. It read 4521 as "four thousand five hundred twenty, one", pause included, and turned the phone number 555-0142 into a subtraction. Spanish text bypasses that step, and "1.249,99 euros, un 12,5 %" turned into nonsense. Spelling English numbers as words did not help. Check every price by ear.
  • Tags by language. The authors document tags for English and Chinese. We only tried them in English, so tags in Spanish text remain untested.
  • The OpenAI speech route. OpenAI-style apps request speech from a dedicated endpoint, which on InferenceKey cannot yet carry a custom backend's audio (open, IK-531). The example goes through the chat route and decodes the WAV out of the message text.

What the test does and does not show

We ran each clip through Whisper, OpenAI's speech-to-text model: 17 of 19 lines matched word for word across English, Spanish and Chinese, and both misses were numbers. A speaker-recognition model rated the clones 0.87 in English and 0.84 in Spanish, both cloned from an English reference. Keep in mind that Ming relies on that same model to capture a voice, which tilts the score towards Ming. No human listened, each line ran once, and the reference was a clean synthetic clip from Kyutai's Pocket TTS. The backend handles a single request at once, so concurrent load is untested.

My read: good for recorded narration, wrong for a live voice agent. If you need Spanish speed more than cloning or tags, our Spanish Pocket TTS voice on CPU reached 1.05x real time on a desktop CPU. Nobody has compared the two for quality.

From empty caches, the backend was ready to serve after 60.3 seconds, about half of it installing Python libraries. The article's appendix has the setup, per-request tables and VRAM ladder for Ming-3.0-tts.

Credit for the model goes to inclusionAI at Ant Group, to OpenAI for Whisper, to Kyutai, who made Pocket TTS, and to the AI Search channel, whose news video pointed us to Ming. The SDK example, the audio samples and every measurement are in the Ming-3.0-tts research article on inferencekey.com.

title: My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight
summary:
My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight

Every Monday morning, someone in leadership asks why a regional revenue metric dropped, and an analyst spends two hours checking the exact same five tables in the exact same order. When we first wired an LLM tool-calling agent to automate root-cause investigations, it had an infuriating habit: it treated every single alert like its first day on the job.

If the South region experienced three consecutive pricing-tier drops over three weeks, a stateless agent would still burn time querying holiday calendars, competitor promo trackers, and warehouse stockout logs before checking pricing. Worse, if the Monday morning ETL sync stalled at 02:00 UTC, the agent would panic over incomplete tables and report a fake revenue collapse. And no matter how many times the Finance Head asked for a single-line summary with the exact dollar variance, the next session returned a multi-paragraph essay.

To fix this, we built WhyDesk—an autonomous metric investigation system powered by FastAPI, Groq tool-calling, and the Hindsight GitHub repository. Instead of treating memory as a passive chat log, we used Vectorize agent memory to dynamically reorder diagnostic tool execution, skip low-probability checks, flag flaky data pipelines before trusting raw numbers, and enforce stakeholder-specific output formatting.

What the System Does and How It Hangs Together

WhyDesk sits between business stakeholders (Finance Head and Senior Analyst) and five deterministic diagnostic tools that inspect weekly regional performance across South, North, West, and East:

  • check_holiday_calendar: Audits regional banking holidays and seasonal B2B checkout dips.
  • check_competitor_promos: Scans market intelligence feeds for aggressive rival discounting.
  • check_inventory_stockouts: Inspects warehouse SKU depletion and unfulfilled hardware bundle backlogs.
  • check_pricing_changes: Audits contract repricing, partner promo codes, discount overrides, and unit ACV shifts.
  • check_etl_pipeline: Verifies warehouse sync completion, job timestamps, and missing row counts.

When an investigation request arrives at POST /api/investigate, WhyDesk does not immediately hand the five tool schemas to the LLM. Instead, it executes a four-stage loop built around the primitives described in what Hindsight does:

User Query + Stakeholder Role
       │
       ▼
1. Hindsight Recall (world, experience, observation) + Reflect
       │
       ▼
2. Memory-Driven Tool Planner (Groq qwen/qwen3-32b -> openai/gpt-oss-120b -> llama-3.3-70b-versatile)
   [Reorders diagnostic tools & enables early stopping once root cause + clean ETL are verified]
       │
       ▼
3. Deterministic Tool Execution + Numeric Grounding Verification
       │
       ▼
4. Synchronous Hindsight Retain (Confirmed cause, ruled-out theories, pipeline reliability, format rule)

Core Technical Story: Turning Memory Into Tool Execution Order

Most agent implementations stuff retrieved text chunks into a prompt and hope the model changes its behavior. In data analysis, passive context is not enough. We needed institutional memory to govern which diagnostic tools run first, which tools get skipped, and how the final answer is shaped.

We organized our Hindsight memory bank (whydesk-bank) around three memory types and configured the bank disposition with high skepticism and literalism (skepticism: 4, literalism: 4, empathy: 2) so confirmed metric verdicts always outweigh unverified guesses:

  1. World facts (world): Confirmed historical root causes and explicitly falsified hypotheses for a region or product line (for example, "In W10 and W12 for the South region, revenue drops were caused by pricing configuration changes; holiday and competitor promo hypotheses were ruled out").
  2. Operational experiences (experience): Lessons learned about data source reliability (for example, "Monday revenue drops in W11 were false alarms caused by an etl_sales_sync warehouse stall; always verify ETL pipeline status before trusting Monday numbers").
  3. Stakeholder observations (observation): Reporting rules per persona (for example, "Stakeholder 'Finance Head' strictly requires a 1-line summary with the exact dollar impact").

1. Pre-Investigation Recall and Reflection (backend/memory.py)

Before calling Groq, WhyDeskMemory.recall_context() queries Hindsight across all three memory types and runs reflect() to synthesize a tactical plan for the current investigation:

def recall_context(self, question: str, region: str, stakeholder: str) -> dict:
    query = (
        f"Past metric investigations for region {region}, reliable vs unreliable data sources, "
        f"ruled out causes, and formatting preferences for stakeholder {stakeholder}. "
        f"Question: {question}"
    )
    recall_resp = self.client.recall(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=query,
        types=["world", "experience", "observation"],
        budget="mid",
        max_tokens=2048,
    )

    memories = [
        {
            "id": getattr(r, "id", ""),
            "text": getattr(r, "text", ""),
            "type": getattr(r, "type", "world"),
            "context": getattr(r, "context", ""),
        }
        for r in (recall_resp.results or [])
    ]

    reflect_resp = self.client.reflect(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=(
            f"Based on past investigations in {region} and stakeholder {stakeholder}: "
            f"1) Which diagnostic tools should run first? "
            f"2) Which hypotheses were repeatedly ruled out? "
            f"3) Any data pipeline traps to check first? "
            f"4) How should the final response for {stakeholder} be formatted?"
        ),
        budget="low",
    )

    return {
        "query": query,
        "memories": memories,
        "reflection": getattr(reflect_resp, "text", ""),
    }

2. Memory-Driven Tool Ordering and Early Stopping (backend/agent.py)

Rather than hardcoding regional rules in Python, backend/agent.py derives the diagnostic execution queue strictly from the recalled memory text and reflection output. On a cold start (0 recalled memories) or when the user switches the UI toggle to Memory off, the agent runs all five tools in the default baseline sequence (check_holiday_calendar -> check_competitor_promos -> check_inventory_stockouts -> check_pricing_changes -> check_etl_pipeline).

When Memory on is active and Hindsight returns prior investigations, the planner scores each diagnostic tool based on recalled pipeline warnings, historical regional root causes, and previously ruled-out checks:

def derive_tool_order_from_memory(memories: list[dict], reflection: str) -> list[str]:
    combined = " ".join(m.get("text", "") for m in memories) + " " + (reflection or "")
    text = combined.lower()

    if not text.strip():
        return list(DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER)

    priority_scores = {tool: 0 for tool in DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER}

    if "etl" in text or "pipeline" in text or "sync" in text or "lag" in text:
        priority_scores["check_etl_pipeline"] += 30
    if "pricing" in text or "discount" in text or "promo code" in text or "repricing" in text:
        priority_scores["check_pricing_changes"] += 20
    if "stockout" in text or "inventory" in text:
        priority_scores["check_inventory_stockouts"] += 15
    if "ruled out" in text and "holiday" in text:
        priority_scores["check_holiday_calendar"] -= 10
    if "ruled out" in text and "competitor" in text:
        priority_scores["check_competitor_promos"] -= 10

    return sorted(
        DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER,
        key=lambda t: (-priority_scores[t], DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER.index(t)),
    )

Once the prioritized tools run, the agent checks whether the warehouse ETL sync is verified clean and a primary anomaly (status == "anomaly_detected") has been isolated. When both conditions are met under memory-guided execution, the loop stops early and skips the remaining low-probability checks.

3. Synchronous Post-Investigation Retention (backend/memory.py)

In an interactive analytics workflow, an analyst often runs follow-up investigations seconds apart. If memory ingestion happens asynchronously in the background, the very next query might miss the finding that was just confirmed. We set retain_async=False on every client.retain() call so verdicts, pipeline notes, and stakeholder preferences are immediately searchable:

self.client.retain(
    bank_id=self.bank_id,
    content=(
        f"In {week} for the {region} region, the confirmed root cause of the revenue anomaly "
        f"was {confirmed_cause} (Impact: {dollar_impact}). "
        f"Ruled-out hypotheses: {', '.join(ruled_out) if ruled_out else 'None'}."
    ),
    context=f"investigation_verdict:{region}",
    timestamp=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    metadata={"region": region, "week": week, "verdict": "confirmed"},
    retain_async=False,
)

Concrete Results: 5-Run Progression and Memory On vs. Off

To verify that every behavioral change comes strictly from stored memories, we ran a five-investigation progression starting from an empty memory bank:

Run Scenario & Stakeholder Recalled Memories Tools Executed (In Order) Tools Count Result & Behavior
Run 1 W10 South (-18%) — Finance Head 0 (Cold Start) holiday -> competitor -> inventory -> pricing -> etl 5 / 5 Finds 20% discount tier (-$42,500). Retains verdict + Finance Head's 1-line rule.
Run 2 W11-Mon South (-64%) — Senior Analyst 2 pricing -> etl 2 / 5 Discovers etl_sales_sync stalled at 02:00 UTC ($0 real loss). Retains ETL lag warning.

title: Why Naive Text Extraction Destroys RAG on Multi-Column PDFs (and How to Fix Reading Order)
summary:
When an AI retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline hallucinates on a question sourced from a scientific paper or financial report, the debugging process almost invariably looks at the wrong layer. Engineers test alternative embedding models, tweak chunk token budgets, or introduce expensive cross-encoder rerankers.

Yet in a surprising fraction of failure cases, the corruption happens before embedding: in the text extraction layer where the parser attempts to reconstruct human reading order from a format that was never designed to store it.

What a PDF File Actually Stores

A PDF is essentially a set of rendering commands designed to place ink or pixels consistently across any screen or printer. Under the hood, text lives inside stream operators bracketed by BT (Begin Text) and ET (End Text):

BT
  /F1 11 Tf
  72 700 Td
  [(Retrieval) -250 (augmented) -250 (generation)] TJ
  0 -14 Td
  (depends on document layout.) Tj
ET

Here, Td moves the coordinate cursor, Tj outputs raw glyph codes, and TJ outputs strings separated by numerical kerning shifts. Crucially:

  1. There is no concept of a "sentence" or "paragraph" in an untagged PDF stream.
  2. The order of rendering commands in the file reflects the sequence in which the generator tool drew elements—not necessarily how a human reads them.
  3. Kerning offsets (like the -250 in the example above) are horizontal spacing nudges, leaving the parser to guess where word spaces belong.

When you pass this document to an automated parser, the tool must guess which glyphs form words, which words form lines, and in what order those lines should be concatenated.

The Multi-Column Braiding Problem

The most damaging extraction error occurs in two-column or multi-column layouts—the standard format for arXiv papers, IEEE publications, and corporate annual reports.

When an extraction library attempts to "fix" raw stream order by sorting text visually by vertical position ($y$-coordinate), it reads across both columns simultaneously. Line 1 of column A is followed immediately by line 1 of column B, then line 2 of column A, then line 2 of column B:

Column A:                          Column B:
Rats were fed a                    All authors declare
standard chow diet                 no competing
for fourteen days.                 financial interests.

Result of naive Y-coordinate sorting:
"Rats were fed a All authors declare standard chow diet no competing for fourteen days. financial interests."

This resulting text is insidious because it never throws a Python exception, passes character-count heuristics, and retains plausible English vocabulary. But when this chunk is sliced into a 512-token window and passed to an embedding model, the vector represents a semantic blend of laboratory protocol and financial disclosures. The vector sits in embedding space near neither topic, making accurate retrieval mathematically impossible.

Three Practical Tiers to Recover Reading Order

Depending on your pipeline constraints and throughput requirements, here are three practical engineering approaches for handling multi-column documents:

Tier 1: Geometric Block Partitioning with Vertical Banding

If you run lightweight CPU-only ingestion using libraries like PyMuPDF (fitz), you can operate on layout bounding boxes (blocks) rather than flat character dumps.

A common naive heuristic splits the page at the horizontal midpoint, but that fails when full-width titles, abstracts, or wide tables appear in the middle of a page. A more robust approach groups blocks into vertical bands separated by spanning elements:

# Practical 2-column reading order parser with vertical band guards
def extract_two_column_page(page, span_threshold=0.75):
    """
    Extracts text from a two-column page while preserving reading sequence.
    Groups text into vertical bands whenever a full-width block appears
    (e.g., page title, abstract, or full-width table/figure), preventing
    mid-page spanning elements from corrupting the sequence.
    """
    # PyMuPDF block format: (x0, y0, x1, y1, text, block_no, block_type)
    # block_type == 0 represents text blocks
    text_blocks = [b for b in page.get_text("blocks") if b[6] == 0]
    if not text_blocks:
        return ""

    page_width = page.rect.width
    midpoint = page_width / 2.0

    # Sort blocks by top coordinate to process page bands top-to-bottom
    text_blocks.sort(key=lambda b: b[1])

    ordered_blocks = []
    current_left = []
    current_right = []

    def flush_columns():
        nonlocal current_left, current_right, ordered_blocks
        if current_left:
            ordered_blocks.extend(sorted(current_left, key=lambda b: b[1]))
            current_left = []
        if current_right:
            ordered_blocks.extend(sorted(current_right, key=lambda b: b[1]))
            current_right = []

    for b in text_blocks:
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = b[0], b[1], b[2], b[3]
        box_width = x1 - x0

        # Spanning elements act as horizontal barriers between column bands
        if box_width >= page_width * span_threshold:
            flush_columns()
            ordered_blocks.append(b)
        elif x0 < midpoint:
            current_left.append(b)
        else:
            current_right.append(b)

    flush_columns()

    return "\n\n".join(b[4].strip() for b in ordered_blocks if b[4].strip())

Note: In production environments with varying margins or 3-column formats, dynamic gutter detection via horizontal projection profiles replaces the static midpoint.

Tier 2: Layout-Aware Vision and Segmentation Models

When documents include irregular multi-column grids, floating callout boxes, and complex multi-row tables, geometric heuristics begin to accumulate edge-case failures.

Layout-aware vision models (such as Docling, Marker, or layout segmentation vision transformers) treat the rendered page as a visual artifact. These architectures predict semantic regions (headings, captions, body paragraphs, tables) and explicitly infer the reading order graph between bounding boxes before converting elements into structured Markdown.

This approach requires significantly higher compute (typically GPU acceleration), but it prevents table rows from collapsing into unstructured text strings.

Tier 3: Producer-Side Tagged PDFs

If your team produces the documents entering the RAG corpus (e.g., internal research memos or documentation exports), the cleanest long-term solution is emitting Tagged PDF (PDF/UA or ISO 32000 tagged structures).

Tagged PDFs embed a structural logical tree directly into the file container, explicitly specifying reading sequence regardless of visual layout positioning. This eliminates heuristic guesswork for both screen readers and downstream AI extractors.

Audit Checklist Before Benchmarking Embedding Models

Before spending budget on new embedding endpoints or vector database re-indexing, run this quick quality audit on your raw text chunks:

  1. Spot-check multi-column transitions: Extract 20 random pages from multi-column documents and check whether sentences jump horizontally across columns.
  2. Inspect table headers: Confirm whether numbers in parsed output remain linked to their column and row descriptors or have flattened into meaningless lists of floats.
  3. Verify formula integrity: Check whether mathematical symbols and sub/superscripts maintain syntactic continuity or fragment across line breaks.
  4. Compare coordinate-sorted vs. raw output: A substantial divergence in text sequence often highlights where layout heuristics are struggling.

Clean document structure upstream is the most reliable foundation for downstream retrieval accuracy.

title: Turning polled battery readings into charge sessions, and flagging the ones you only half saw
summary:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of ScooterLog, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the app's source code. ScooterLog is an independent app, not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Ola Electric.

ScooterLog shows every charge in a timeline: start and end percent, how long it took, when it reached 100%. No system hands us that list. The scooter's cloud reports a current state, the server polls it every few minutes, and a "charge" is something we have to reconstruct from a row of samples.

The reconstruction is about 40 lines of Python and SQLite. The interesting part is less the state machine than being honest about what the samples can't tell you.

The input

Each poll produces a reading, stored once:

CREATE TABLE history(
    user_id TEXT, vehicle_id TEXT, source_ms INTEGER,
    battery_soc REAL, charging_state TEXT, odometer REAL,
    -- ...
    PRIMARY KEY(user_id, vehicle_id, source_ms));

source_ms is the timestamp the upstream attached to the reading, not the time we fetched it. That choice does a lot of work, because a poll can return the same reading again:

cur = c.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO history(...) VALUES (...)', (...))
new = cur.rowcount > 0
if new:
    _update_charging(c, user_id, vehicle_id, point)

A repeat insert changes nothing, so the session logic only runs on genuinely new information. Downstream, alarm checks hang off the same return value, so a reading can't trigger them twice.

The state machine has no explicit state

There are two ingredients: is this reading charging, and is there an open session row (end_ms IS NULL)? That gives three actions, and the fourth combination does nothing:

charging = state in ('SLOW_CHARGING', 'FAST_CHARGING')

if charging and not openrow:      # open: record start time, %, odometer
    ...
elif charging and openrow:        # extend: update end %, keep it open
    ...
elif not charging and openrow:    # close: record end time, %, odometer
    ...

The "state" is just the database. A server restart in the middle of a charge loses nothing, since the next reading finds the open row and carries on.

Two details are easy to get wrong. A charge that moves from slow to fast is one session, not two, because both states count as charging. The test pins this down:

pts = [

    {'source_ms': 3, 'battery_soc': 55, 'charging_state': 'FAST_CHARGING'},
    {'source_ms': 4, 'battery_soc': 80, 'charging_state': 'NOT_CHARGING'},

Say you read 40% and charging, then the server is down for three hours, then you read 100% and not charging. The naive result is a three-hour session. The truth might be a 90-minute charge and 90 minutes sitting at full. Nothing in the data distinguishes them.

closing The unplug may have happened any time in the gap, so the duration may be too long

WHERE user_id=? AND vehicle_id=? AND start_ms=?

COALESCE handles older rows from before the column existed. The bitwise OR means a later clean reading can't wash the flag away.

title: Planning an AI short-drama pipeline without buying a new GPU
summary:
Before buying more hardware for AI video, compare the cost of upgrading with renting for the stages that need a GPU. Our ep05 explainer discusses that decision (video link below); this article proposes a workflow, not a completed production benchmark.

If you would rather defer a hardware purchase, one possible setup is to run the light stages through an API and rent a GPU for the stages that need your own model weights.

Untested example: The snippets below were checked against public documentation, not executed. They are illustrative, not a tested end-to-end workflow; add error handling, timeouts and output checks before use. Catalog presence is not proof of successful inference or current GPU stock.

The pipeline, stage by stage

An episode of a vertical short drama (a minute or two, 15–30 shots) breaks down like this:

Stage What runs Where it runs well
Series bible + episode script a large chat model API
Shot list + image/video prompts a fast chat model API
Keyframes / character sheets FLUX API, or ComfyUI on a GPU if you use a character LoRA
Shots Model supporting the required input API for supported shots; custom ComfyUI workflows on a GPU sized for the workload
Voice TTS API
Subtitles Whisper API

The rule of thumb: anything stateless and prompt-driven goes to an API. Anything that needs your weights (a character LoRA, a custom ComfyUI graph) goes on a GPU you control, for as long as the render takes.

1. Script and shot list over an OpenAI-compatible API

The OpenAI Python and Node SDKs are documented for chat completions with a CloudGPU base URL and key; that does not imply every SDK feature is supported. A large model writes the episode and a fast one turns it into shots:

import os, json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://cloudgpu.app/v1",
)

bible = open("series_bible.md").read()   # characters, tone, recurring props

episode = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-pro",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You write 90-second vertical drama episodes. Keep names and facts consistent with the bible."},
        {"role": "user", "content": bible + "\n\nWrite episode 4: the sister finds the letter."},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-flash",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": 'Split the script into shots. Return {"shots":[{"id":1,"seconds":4,"image_prompt":"...","motion_prompt":"...","line":"..."}]}'},
        {"role": "user", "content": episode},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = json.loads(shots)["shots"]
print(len(shots), "shots")

Keep the bible as a file in the repo and send it with every episode. It can help consistency, but review each generated script; it is not a guarantee.

2. Quick shots through the video endpoint

For establishing shots and B-roll that don't need a locked character, a video job is enough. It's asynchronous: create, poll, download.

import time, requests

H = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"]}
BASE = "https://cloudgpu.app/v1"

job = requests.post(f"{BASE}/videos", headers=H, json={
    "model": "wan-3.0",
    "prompt": shots[0]["image_prompt"] + ". " + shots[0]["motion_prompt"],
}).json()

while True:
    status = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}", headers=H).json()["status"]
    if status in ("completed", "failed"):
        break
    time.sleep(10)

if status == "completed":
    mp4 = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}/content", headers=H)
    open("shot_01.mp4", "wb").write(mp4.content)

Optional fields (resolution, seconds, and image for models that accept images) are listed in the API docs. The current catalog lists wan-3.0 as text-to-video only; use an image-capable model for image-to-video. Finished files are downloadable for 24 hours, so pull them into your own storage.

3. Character shots on a rented GPU

When the lead has to look the same in every shot, you want your own LoRA and your own ComfyUI graph. VRAM requirements depend on the workflow, precision, resolution and offloading. CloudGPU's published Wan 2.2 test reports about 21 GB peak VRAM for its tested 14B FP8 configuration; do not treat 24 GB or 48 GB as a universal requirement.

Instead of buying that card, start one only for the render batch. The GPU API documents server-enforced auto-shutdown limits. Set and monitor appropriate limits; they do not replace copying outputs before destruction:

templates = requests.get(f"{BASE}/gpu/templates", headers=H).json()
comfy = next(t for t in templates["data"] if "comfyui" in t["name"].lower())

inst = requests.post(f"{BASE}/gpu/instances", headers=H, json={
    "template": comfy["id"],
    "gpu_model": "auto",       # or pick a card from GET /gpu/offers
    "idle_minutes": 30,        # destroy after 30 idle minutes
    "max_minutes": 240,        # hard cap for this batch
}).json()
print(inst["id"], inst["status"])

Then SSH in, pull your LoRA and workflow, queue the shots, copy the MP4s out, and destroy the instance (DELETE /gpu/instances/{id}). Billing is per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum; billing stops when you destroy the instance. Check the live deploy page for which cards are available that day.

(The response shape above is simplified; check GET /v1/gpu/templates once and adjust the field names to what it returns.)

4. Voice and subtitles

Both are OpenAI-format audio endpoints, so the same client works:

speech = client.audio.speech.create(model="kokoro-tts", voice="af_heart", input=shots[0]["line"])
speech.write_to_file("line_01.mp3")

with open("episode_04_rough.mp4", "rb") as f:
    srt = client.audio.transcriptions.create(model="whisper-v3-turbo", file=f, response_format="srt")
open("episode_04.srt", "w").write(srt)

(Voice names depend on the TTS model; list them from the docs.)

Rent or buy?

We won't quote prices here because they move. Do the math with your own numbers:

  • Hours per month you actually need a big card (renders + LoRA training, not editing).
  • The card's local price today, plus the RAM and SSD you'd also upgrade.
  • How long until you'd upgrade again.

If the big-card hours are a few sessions a month, renting keeps the money in your pocket and nothing sits idle. Daily rendering can change the calculation; compare hardware, electricity, utilization and cloud costs rather than assuming buying always wins.

That's also the takeaway from ep05: buy what you need, don't hoard, and for the occasional big job, rent the kitchen instead of building one.

  • Video: Will phones and computers cost more next year? — https://youtu.be/XSiCDC8v18Y
  • Per-stage GPU guide for short dramas: https://cloudgpu.app/cloud-gpu-for-ai-short-drama?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg03_freelancer_gpu_api&utm_content=devto_drama_pipeline_rent

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU. The API and GPU calls above are CloudGPU's; the pipeline is a proposal, and endpoint, model and GPU capabilities differ by provider. Pay by card or USDT; see /payments for the current list of methods.

Sources checked 2026-11-07: API docs, model catalog, billing terms, published short-drama workflow and test settings.

title: The Life of a Django Request
summary:
A guided tour of everything that happens between someone clicking a link and your view function running. No traps, no gotchas, just how it actually works.

Most articles about Django are about what goes wrong. This one isn't. This is a tour.

Every time someone loads a page in your Django app, a small, elegant machine springs into motion. It unwraps the request, threads it through a stack of layers, finds the right view, runs your code, and packages the answer back up, usually in well under a tenth of a second.

Most of us write views for years without ever watching that machine run. We know our view function gets called with a request object, and we know we return a response, and the space between is a comfortable fog.

Let's clear the fog. We're going to follow a single request from the instant it leaves a browser to the instant the response arrives back, and at each stop I'll show you what Django is actually doing and why.

By the end, request and response won't be magic. They'll be things you understand from the inside. That understanding is quietly one of the most useful things you can have as a Django developer, because once you can see the machine, you know exactly where to reach when something needs explaining, debugging, or extending.

Here's the whole journey at a glance, and then we'll walk it step by step:

Browser → Nginx → Gunicorn (WSGI) → Django handler
      → Middleware (in) → URL resolver → Your view (ORM + templates)
      → Middleware (out) → Gunicorn → Nginx → Browser

Stop 1: The Browser and the Web Server

It starts with a browser making an HTTP request (GET /articles/42/) and sending it across the internet to your server. The first thing it hits isn't Django at all. It's a web server, typically Nginx, sitting at the front door.

Nginx handles the things Django shouldn't be bothered with:

  • Serving static files (CSS, images) directly
  • Terminating SSL
  • Load-balancing across multiple app processes

For anything dynamic (anything that needs your code), Nginx hands the request off to an application server like Gunicorn or uWSGI.

Think of Nginx as the receptionist who deals with routine visitors themselves and only forwards the real business inward.

So already there are two programs involved before Django wakes up. This is worth knowing, because when people say "Django is slow to serve static files" or debug a deployment, the answer usually lives right here in the handoff between the web server and the app server.

Stop 2: WSGI, the Universal Handshake

Gunicorn now has the request, but Gunicorn and Django are separate projects written by different people. How do they talk? Through a contract called WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface), and understanding this contract demystifies a huge amount.

WSGI is dead simple. The server calls your application as a plain function with two arguments:

  • environ: a dictionary holding everything about the request (the path, headers, method, all of it)
  • start_response: a callback for setting the status and headers

Your application does its work and returns the response body as bytes.

That's the entire contract. And it's why you can run Django under Gunicorn or uWSGI or others interchangeably. They all speak WSGI, so any of them can talk to any WSGI framework.

Django's end of this handshake lives in a file you've seen and probably never opened: wsgi.py. That file exposes a WSGIHandler, the object Gunicorn calls. This is the true front door of Django itself.

title: 5 Python PDF libraries vs 1,068 broken PDFs: what crashed, and why one of my explanations was wrong
summary:
I fed 1,068 broken PDFs to five Python libraries and asked each one for the text. The files are Mozilla's pdf.js test suite: PDFs people attached to bug reports over the years, with broken cross-reference tables, strange fonts and fuzzed bytes. If your code reads PDFs that strangers upload, these are the files that will eventually reach it.

Library Failed* Failed where 3+ others worked Total time Slowest file
PyMuPDF 2.1 5 2 14 s 5.9 s
pypdfium2 5.14.0 14 2 6 s 0.6 s
pypdf 6.21.4 23 7 83 s 13.8 s
pdfminer.six 20260107 22 6 204 s timeout (60 s)
pdfplumber 0.11.10 23 7 225 s timeout (60 s)

* Raised an error or hit the 60-second limit. Not counted: 12 password-protected files that at least two libraries reported as needing a password. Python 3.13, 2-vCPU ARM server, each library in its own worker processes.

The fast two are 6 to 40 times faster

pypdfium2 got through all 1,068 files in 6 seconds. PyMuPDF needed 14. pypdf took 83, pdfminer.six 204, and pdfplumber 225, which is almost four minutes for the same pile.

pdfplumber's worst file was freeculture.pdf, a 352-page book. It hit my 60-second limit, while pdfminer.six, the parser pdfplumber is built on, reads the same book in about 12 seconds. So the time goes into pdfplumber's own layout work. If you only need the text, you don't need pdfplumber.

pdfplumber is not a fallback for pdfminer.six

Five of their unique failures are the same files, often with the same error ('PDFObjRef' object is not subscriptable). That makes sense once you know pdfplumber uses pdfminer.six to parse. If you want a second library to catch what the first one drops, pick one with a different parser.

pypdfium2 is the easiest one to build a fallback around. 22 of its 24 failures happen right when it opens the file ("Data format error"), so you find out at once and can hand the file to something else.

The π file, and the explanation I had to take back

pdf.js has a test file, filled-background.pdf, stuffed with 100,000-digit numbers: π, in three objects and again in a comment inside the cross-reference table. pypdf stops with LimitReachedError (it refuses numbers longer than 64 characters). The other four libraries read it.

My first write-up said the comment alone was the culprit. While preparing this post I tested that, by deleting the comment line. pypdf still failed with the same error. Shortening every digit run turned it into a different error from the same xref parser. So this file trips pypdf in more than one way, and my neat one-line cause was wrong. I've fixed the original note.

The other lesson from this run was about timeouts. An earlier harness of mine used a Python alarm signal to stop slow files. One file sat inside C code for 44 minutes and the alarm never fired. Now every library runs in a worker process that gets killed from outside.

Only one readable file beat all five libraries: poppler-742-0-fuzzed.pdf. Five more failed everywhere, but they're encrypted.

This only says whether a library breaks, not how good its text is. Reading order, spacing and tables are a separate test. About 350 to 390 files gave no text in every library, mostly because they hold only images or shapes. And check the licences: PyMuPDF is AGPL or commercial, the other four are permissive.

Run it yourself

The harness is corpusdiff, a small open-source tool I wrote for this kind of test:

git clone https://github.com/prometheus-maker/corpusdiff && cd corpusdiff
pip install . pymupdf pypdfium2 pypdf pdfplumber
corpusdiff fetch pdfjs corpora/pdfjs
corpusdiff run examples/pdf_libs.py:pypdf_text corpora/pdfjs -o pypdf.jsonl -t 60
corpusdiff summary pypdf.jsonl

If you spot a mistake, say so in the comments and I'll correct the post. The original version lives on my notes site.

title: A vendor claimed +90.2% annualised. Their own monthly table says 34.8% without three months.
summary:
Last week a trading-platform newsletter landed in my inbox with a strategy of the week.

The headline: Hypothetical Annual Return (Compounded) +90.2%. Somewhere above it, in smaller type: "All results are hypothetical."

I do not know whether the strategy works. I do know that a monthly percentage table is enough to check the arithmetic, so I checked it.

The table

Two and a bit years of monthly cells, printed right there in the email:

Year months (%)
2024 -3.8, +8.3, -0.5, -7.9, +5.3, +3.9, +4.5
2025 +8.5, +0.1, +0.6, +50.7, +7.6, +4.5, +3.3, +10.9, -, +6.2, +12.4, +10.7
2026 +14.1, +23.4, -20.9, +20.3, -6.1, -8.9, -3.9, +2.8, +9.3, +18.5, +2.2, +50.1

Compound them:

  • 2024 (7 months): +9.16%
  • 2025 (11 months, September missing): +180.27% — the email prints +180.4%
  • 2026 (11 months): +49.9% — the email prints +50.1%
  • Full span: roughly +350%, which annualises to ~90.3%

So the +90.2% is not a typo and not a fabrication. The arithmetic holds. That is the part almost nobody checks, and it passed.

What the arithmetic hides

Three questions turn "consistent" into "informative".

1. How much rests on a few months?

The three largest cells are +50.7%, +23.4%, +50.1%. Remove those three months and the annualised figure falls to about 34.8%. The strategy is not a smooth 90% engine; it is a handful of good months carrying a decade of averages.

2. What is the worst peak-to-trough on monthly closes?

-21.8%. And 2026 contains -20.9%, then -6.1%, -8.9%, -3.9% in a row. Anyone sizing this needs to know that sequence exists before they read the annualised number.

3. What exactly is being measured?

The vendor's own disclaimer: "there is no single real-life trading account that looks exactly like the track record shown here." Fees are estimated, not taken from a broker statement. The track record is a model account.

None of that is fraud. It is a hypothetical number, clearly labelled as such, in 8-point type.

The three-question check

For any seller quoting an annualised return:

  1. Ask for the monthly cells, not the annual figure.
  2. Compound them yourself. If it does not match, stop and ask why. If it matches, continue.
  3. Drop the three best months and recompute; compute the worst monthly peak-to-trough.

Two minutes, a calculator, and you learn whether the number is durable or decorative.

I keep the working notes and a small standard-library toolkit for this kind of check in backtest-audit-kit. The write-up for this case is case 15.

If you sell a strategy and your numbers survive these three questions, say so — that is rarer than a 90% headline.

title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: How Small Models + Skillware Beat Frontier LLMs
summary:
Stop forcing LLMs to write disposable Python scripts on the fly. Here is how deterministic capability bundles slash token burn by 84.8%, cut costs by 97.3%, and let 8B local models outperform GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 5.

Right now, the AI engineering world is trapped in a very expensive delusion: the prompt-driven execution paradigm.

We give an auto-regressive language model a massive markdown dump of API docs, tell it to dynamically synthesize Python or bash scripts on the fly, and pray that it respects security boundaries because we wrote "IMPORTANT: DO NOT DELETE PROD" in all caps in the system prompt.

When it works, it feels like magic. When it hits production, it's a disaster. You get Prompt Rot (switching models breaks all your tool shims), Quadratic Attention Tax (paying frontier rates to re-read static OpenAPI schemas on every turn), and the dreaded Context Poisoning Cliff—where an agent fails a script attempt, dumps a massive stack trace into its own context window, and spirals into terminal hallucination by attempt #8.

In a new paper from ARPA Hellenic Logical Systems ("Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems", arXiv:2611.07652v1, we formalize the antidote: Capability Engineering.

The RPG Hotkey Analogy

Think about how skills work in an RPG like Morrowind or Diablo. When your character casts a spell or triggers an ability, you don't open a chat box and negotiate with the game engine to invent the physics of a fireball at runtime.

You press a hotkey. If the preconditions hold (you have the mana, you're outside a sanctuary town, targeting a valid hostile), the engine executes pre-compiled, deterministic logic and produces the exact same state transition every time.

Skillware brings this exact discipline to AI agents:

The Principle of Separation of Cognition and Capability: The model decides when to act and selects the parameters; the capability bundle governs how the action is executed. The assistant is a guest in this case, while the hard function does the work.

What is a Skillware Bundle?

Instead of loose SKILL.md files or brittle prompt wrappers, Skillware packages capabilities into self-contained, versioned, 5-role software bundles:

  1. Contract (manifest.yaml): Typed JSON Schema inputs/outputs, required env vars, cryptographic publisher identity, and an immutable Constitution (e.g., confirmed: true gates for destructive actions).
  2. Effect (skill.py): Pre-compiled, deterministic Python logic subclassing BaseSkill. Zero runtime code synthesis.
  3. Directive (instructions.md): Progressive disclosure guidance loaded Just-In-Time (JIT) only when needed.
  4. Assurance (test_skill.py): Hermetic offline pytest suites that verify the Effect honors the Contract in <100ms without calling a single LLM API.
  5. Corpus & Presentation (data/, card.json): Static offline datasets (like OFAC sanctions lists or statutory lexicons) bundled right next to the code for 100% air-gapped execution.

Universal In-Process Adapters (Zero IPC Latency)

Unlike MCP (which requires spinning up and supervising out-of-process client-server daemons over stdio/HTTP sockets), Skillware executes in-process in CPython in <1.2ms. Its universal interface morphisms (to_gemini_tool(), to_claude_tool(), to_openai_tool(), to_ollama_prompt()) automatically translate your manifest.yaml into any provider's native tool dialect on the fly.

from skillware.core import SkillLoader

# 1. Load a verified, offline-tested capability bundle
bundle = SkillLoader.load_skill("finance/wallet_screening")
skill = bundle["class"]()

# 2. Auto-transmute contract to host dialect (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Ollama)
tools = [SkillLoader.to_gemini_tool(bundle)]

# 3. Pre-flight AST schema validation + deterministic local execution
try:
    result = skill.execute(dict(call.args))
except SkillwareParamValidationError as exc:
    result = {"error": f"Invalid arguments: {exc}"}

The SLM Parameter Paradox: 8B Local > Frontier Cloud

We evaluated 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions (SKILLWARE-BENCH), testing multi-step email handling, UK corporate registry resolution, on-chain sanctions screening, and adversarial prompt injection.

The headline finding? The SLM Parameter Paradox.

When you stop forcing models to write disposable code and restrict them strictly to semantic routing and schema parameter selection, 3B–8B local models equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier giants (including GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 5):

  • 97.3% Cost Reduction: Dropping from $15.58 (Frontier LLM dynamically writing code) to $0.42 per 1,000 turns using a local 8B SLM + Skillware.
  • 84.0% Context Excision: Progressive JIT disclosure (mode="brief") compresses tool signatures to ~30 tokens, slashing total token burn by up to 84.8%.
  • Zero Parameter Corruption: Pre-flight JSON Schema validation drops parameter errors from 18.5% down to 0.0% and eliminates all 464 runtime script debugging loops.
  • 56.2% Lift for Open-Weight Models: Meta Llama 4 Maverick jumps from a 37.5% pass rate (vanilla) to 93.8% when equipped, while Qwen 3.8 Flash and Gemma 4 (31B) hit 100.0%.
  • 1.2ms Zero-Token Firewall: Instead of using a second LLM to audit incoming text for prompt injection (which doubles your cost and still gets jailbroken), Skillware uses a 3-stage deterministic normalization pipeline (stripping zero-width Unicode smuggling, Cyrillic/Greek homoglyphs, and hidden DOM spans) in 1.2ms with 0 tokens burned.

From Python Loops to Drones and Neural Interfaces

Why does sub-millisecond, in-process determinism matter beyond saving API budget? Because software agents are only Scale I.

Under ISO 13849 SIL-3 safety standards, physical fault mitigation in robotics and industrial Digital Twins must execute within 10ms, and high-frequency robotic/UAV control loops run at 500Hz (1–2ms). You cannot run a drone or a surgical neuroprosthetic over a 2.5-second cloud LLM loop or an out-of-process JSON-RPC socket.

By establishing a formal Clock-Domain Crossing (CDC) between slow cognitive deliberation (~1s) and sub-millisecond deterministic motor schemas (<1.2ms), Skillware lays the foundation for installing verified capabilities across autonomous IoT, embodied robotics, and eventually Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs).

The era of prompt engineering is closing; the era of Capability Engineering has begun. Stop renting disposable logic by the token.
